domain: King of Phrygia, the Golden Touch

phonemes.desc: Bilabial nasal opening into acute-pitched iota [mí] — the name's single mark, pitched high.
Voiced dental stop [d] — plain and firm.
Short alpha and final sigma [as] — the common ending of Anatolian royal names.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MEE-dass' — stress forward, the first syllable bright and the second clipped; the English 'MY-das' flattens both.

kin.label: Assyrian

kin.label: Phrygian

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Μίδας, the Hellenized form, fixed by Herodotus and the myth

pronunciation.note: Mídas is Tier 2 because the Greek Μίδας carries only the acute stress; the vowels are short and no long vowel or diphthong is preserved. Behind the Greek form stands a genuine Phrygian royal name — the legend has a historical king inside it.

domains.title: The Gilded King
domains.subtitle: Kingship, Gold, and the Price of Wishes
domains.lead: Mídas is the double figure of Greek imagination: a real king of Phrygia, known to Assyrian scribes as Mitâ of Muški and to Herodotus as the first foreigner to send gifts to Delphi — and the mythic fool whose wish made the world gold and his stomach empty. In him, legend and chronicle meet like the two halves of a coin.

cards.name: The Golden Touch
cards.desc: Granted by Dionysos in thanks for the return of Silenos; everything his hands touched — bread, wine, roses — hardened into gold.

cards.name: The Judgment of Ears
cards.desc: When he preferred Pan's pipes to Apollo's lyre, Apollo gave him the ears of an ass — the byword for deaf judgment ever since.

cards.name: The Phrygian King
cards.desc: Behind the fable stands a historical ruler of Gordion, contemporary of Sargon II of Assyria, lord of the Phrygian migrations.

cards.name: The River Pactolus
cards.desc: Where he washed away the gift at the god's command; its sands ran gold afterward, the aition of Lydia's wealth.

mythology.lead: The Greeks attached two great fables to Mídas — the touch and the ears — and one genuine history: the wealthy Phrygian king whose gifts reached Delphi and whose wars reached Assyria. Ovid gives the fables their classic form; Herodotus keeps the history.

myths.title: Silenos Returned
myths.text:
In Ovid's telling, the satyr Silenos — foster-father and perpetual companion of Dionysos — strayed from the god's train in Phrygia, drunken and lost, and was found by countrymen who bound him with garlands of flowers and brought him to King Midas. The king knew at once what he had: ten days and ten nights of feasting and storytelling, and then he restored the old satyr to the Bacchic host with honor. Dionysos offered any gift in return, and Midas answered like a treasurer: let everything I touch become gold. The god, who grants what is asked, granted it — 'nor did the god rejoice,' Ovid adds, for the wish told him exactly what its wisher was.

The episode is the guest-gift inverted: hospitality toward the god's companion earns not wisdom but a confirmation of appetite, and the golden touch begins as a reading of the host's character.

myths.title: All He Touches Turns to Gold
myths.text:
The gift revealed itself at table: the bread hardened under his fingers, the wine ran molten from his lips and would not wet them, the rose he plucked glittered stiff and leafless. Rich, and starving in a palace of metal, Midas lifted his arms to heaven — 'Dionysos, father, forgive me; I have sinned' — and the god, relenting, sent him to wash in the spring at the source of the Pactolus near Sardis. The power left his body and entered the river, whose sands have run gold ever after — the aition ancient geographers repeated of Lydia's wealth. Later retellings, from scholia to Nathaniel Hawthorne, add the gilded daughter; antiquity needed no child to make the point.

The myth measures the exact distance between having gold and being fed by it: one wish, granted literally, is a famine in a treasury.

myths.title: The Ears of an Ass
myths.text:
The second fable is a music-contest: the piping Pan dared the lyre of Apollo, and the mountain-god Tmolos judged for the lyre. Midas alone clapped for the pipes, and Apollo's punishment was exact — 'why not,' the god says, 'since your ears are so dull, lengthen them to a donkey's measure?' Under the Phrygian cap the secret grew, but the king's barber saw, and the barber, forbidden to tell, dug a hole in the riverbank and whispered it into the earth. Reeds rose from that ground, and ever after, when the wind combs them, they murmur the truth: King Midas has ass's ears.

The story is a parable of criticism as hearing: the judge of song becomes the judged of ears, and nature itself is recruited as the gossip a court tried to suppress.

myths.title: Mitâ of Muški
myths.text:
Behind both fables stands a king historians can date. The annals of Sargon II of Assyria record Mitâ, king of Muški — the Assyrian name for the Phrygians — who raided the empire's western marches around 718–709 BCE and then sued for alliance, sending tribute and an embassy to Nineveh. Herodotus preserves his splendor: Midas was the first foreigner known to have sent gifts to Delphi, dedicating the royal throne on which suppliants sat, and his name still meant wealth to fifth-century Greeks. Herodotus adds the family memory: the roses below Mount Bermion in Macedon were Midas's gardens, where Silenos was said to have been captured, and the Macedonian royal house counted his gardeners among its ancestors.

The historical Midas thus glitters in three archives — Assyrian, Greek, and Phrygian — and the fable of the golden touch reads, in this light, as a caricature of a man whose wealth was already proverbial.

lore.syncretism: Mídas absorbed no foreign gods; instead, the myth absorbed the man. Greek storytellers took a historical Phrygian dynasty and hung upon it their two great parables of appetite and judgment. Rome passed the fables on in Ovid's polished telling, and in time the moral inverted itself: the 'Midas touch', once a curse, became the financier's compliment. The ass's ears went the other way, remaining exactly what Apollo made them — the emblem of the critic who cannot hear.
lore.culturalLegacy: Few names are so thoroughly proverbial. 'The Midas touch' names effortless profit; 'Midas ears' names the opposite gift in judgment. Hawthorne's A Wonder-Book (1852) added the golden daughter, the version children now learn first; opera, satire, and economics have all mined him. The historical king endures as firmly as the fool: Gordion's excavations made him a fixed point of Iron Age chronology. To restore Mídas with its acute is to restore the Greek shape of a Phrygian name — a small act of hearing rightly, which he himself never managed.
lore.extendedMeditation:
The touch and the ears are one story told twice. Both are parables of misjudged value: the king who thinks gold is the best thing in the world, and the listener who thinks pipes are better than the lyre. Each wish-come-true is a famine; each judgment is a deformity. The Greeks were exact about this — wealth and taste are the two places where a man chooses what he is, and Midas chose wrong both times, and knew it, and wept, and was not destroyed.

For the myth is gentler than its proverb. Dionysos releases him; Apollo only marks him. He washes the gold away in the river and, Ovid says, hated riches ever after — a man cured by his cure. Perhaps that is why a real king's name clung to the fable: the historical Midas was famous for sending his treasures away, a throne across the sea to Delphi. The legend only exaggerates the gesture. He is the king forever giving gold back, and the river still pays it out, grain by grain.

lore.archaeology: Gordion (Yassıhöyük), the Phrygian capital on the Sangarios, has been excavated by the University of Pennsylvania since 1950: the citadel's gate and megarons, and the Great Tumulus (Tumulus MM, ca. 740 BCE) with its preserved wooden chamber and hoard of bronzes — now dated a generation too early for Mídas himself and assigned to his dynasty, most plausibly Gordias his father. Old Phrygian inscriptions name Midas on the rock façade of the 'Midas Monument' at Yazılıkaya and at Midas City. The Assyrian annals of Sargon II supply the external chronicle, naming Mitâ of Muški between 718 and 709 BCE. His ivory throne at Delphi, which Herodotus saw, has not survived.
